title: Every Football Team Destroyed By A Plane Crash
angle: Five aircraft carrying footballers never landed.

sections.title: Every Football Team Destroyed By A Plane Crash
sections.text: Emiliano Raúl Sala Taffarel was born prematurely in the town of Cululú, Santa Fe Province, with concerns that respiratory issues might prevent him from being able to run. Decades later, the newly signed Cardiff City striker vanished over the English Channel in a light aircraft flown by a pilot who had no license to fly at night. He was one of exactly four people who died across these tragedies, while others survived. Months earlier, fans leaving a stadium filmed a helicopter carrying Leicester City's owner as it spun out of control and crashed into the car park. In 1996, a single misread altitude instruction caused the deadliest mid-air collision ever recorded. In 1949, a plane carrying the greatest football team in Italy flew into a hillside behind a basilica, killing the entire squad.

sections.title: The disappearance of Emiliano Sala
sections.text: The disappearance of Argentine footballer Emiliano Sala remains one of the most tragic mysteries in modern sport. Born in Cululú, Sala overcame early respiratory issues to forge a professional career in France. By January 2019, his standout form earned him a club-record fifteen-million-pound transfer to Cardiff City. After briefly returning to Nantes to say goodbye to friends, Sala boarded a Piper Malibu light aircraft on January 21, 2019, to fly back to Cardiff. Two days after signing his landmark contract, the small plane carrying the striker vanished over the English Channel. The pilot had no license to fly at night. An initial three-day search covering four thousand four hundred square kilometres failed to locate the aircraft. Two subsequent private searches were launched to find the missing striker. On February 3, 2019, searchers finally discovered the wreckage of the plane. Sala's body was recovered from the site four days later, confirming the devastating end to his promising life and career.

sections.title: The helicopter crash that killed Leicester City's owner
sections.text: In August 2010, Thai billionaire businessman Vichai Srivaddhanaprabha purchased the English football club Leicester City. Under his ownership, the club achieved a legendary sporting miracle, winning the 2015–16 Premier League title despite starting the season as 5000/1 outsiders. Vichai became a beloved figure, known for his generosity and his close relationship with the fans. On 27 October 2018, he attended a Leicester City match at the club's home ground, King Power Stadium. Minutes after the game concluded, Vichai boarded his AgustaWestland AW169 helicopter, which took off directly from the pitch. As fans were still leaving the area, the aircraft suddenly spun out of control just outside the stadium. Filmed by onlookers, the helicopter crashed into the stadium car park and erupted into a fireball. The following day, officials confirmed that Vichai, the two pilots, and two other passengers had died in the crash. In the wake of the tragedy, grieving players and fans gathered to lay numerous tributes outside the stadium, mourning the sudden loss of the man who had transformed their club.

sections.title: The Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
sections.text: On 12 November 1996, Saudia Flight 763, a Boeing 747 departing Delhi for Dhahran, and Kazakhstan Airlines Flight 1907, an Ilyushin Il-76 arriving from Shymkent, collided mid-air over the Indian city of Charkhi Dadri. The disaster occurred because the Kazakh crew failed to maintain their correct assigned altitude. In the Kazakh cockpit, poor English language skills led to an inadequate interpretation of air traffic control directions, which was compounded by three specific failures in crew resource management. Furthermore, the Indian airport operated with only a primary radar, which could not display aircraft altitude. Unaware of their deadly proximity, the two planes met head-on in the clouds. The impact killed all 349 people on board both aircraft, making it the world's deadliest mid-air collision and the deadliest aviation accident ever in India. In the aftermath, investigators determined that technical enhancements, including secondary surveillance radar and airborne collision avoidance systems, were desperately needed to ensure that future crew mistakes would not go unchecked in real time.

sections.title: The Superga air disaster
sections.text: On May 4, 1949, the legendary Grande Torino football team perished in the Superga air disaster. The squad was flying home to Italy from Lisbon aboard an Avio Linee Italiane Fiat G.212 airliner, following a friendly match against S.L. Benfica. After a refueling stop in Barcelona, where the players shared lunch with the Milan team, the aircraft departed at 14:50 for the Turin-Aeritalia Airport. As the plane approached its destination, the weather in Turin deteriorated rapidly, bringing heavy rain, strong wind gusts, and visibility of just 40 meters. At 16:59, pilot Lieutenant Colonel Meroni reported his altitude at 2,000 meters, planning to cut across Superga. A strong crosswind likely drifted the plane off course, or a malfunctioning altimeter misled the crew about their true height. At 17:03, while aligning for landing in the dense fog, the airliner slammed directly into the retaining wall at the back of the Basilica of Superga, which stood on a hill overlooking Turin. All thirty-one people on board, including eighteen players, coaching staff, club officials, journalists, and crew, were killed instantly.

sections.title: Closing
sections.text: These tragedies left different ruins in their wake. Some investigations found mechanical failures, while others blamed human error in the dark. A few passengers died alone in the sea, while entire clubs vanished together on mountainsides. Yet each disaster stopped the clock for millions of fans at the exact same moment. The sport did not pause because of the shared logistics of travel, but because these men carried the collective imagination of their cities into the air. When they fell, they took a piece of the local sky with them.
